Title: Genetic and Genomic Abnormalities in a Patient with Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
PMID: 
Authors: Christina Kelly, Caitlin Raymond, Song Han, Youmin Lin, Linyijia Chen, Gengming Huang, Jianli Dong

Abstract
Non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) has been found to have recurrent genetic abnormalities, and novel therapies targeting these aberrations have improved patient survival. In this study, specimens from benign tissue, primary tumors, and brain metastases were obtained at autopsy from a 55-year-old White female patient diagnosed with NSCLC and were examined using next-generation sequencing (NGS) and chromosomal microarray assay (CMA). No genetic aberrations were noted in the benign tissue; however, NGS identified a mutation in the KRAS proto-oncogene, GTPase (KRAS): KRAS exon 2 p.G12D in primary and metastatic tumor specimens. We observed 7 DNA copy number aberrations (CNAs) in primary and metastatic tumor specimens; an additional 7 CNAs were exclusively detected in the metastatic tumor specimens. These DNA alterations may be genetic drivers in the pathogenesis of the tumor specimen from our patient and may serve as biomarkers for the classification and prognosis of NSCLC.

Case Presentation
The patient, who had no known previous disease, presented with acute severe leg and back pain. Her surgical history consisted of a right breast tumor that was presumed benign. Her social history included a smoking history of 35 packs of cigarettes per year. Her sister (who had died at age 51) and mother had experienced unspecified lung cancer.
After her symptoms had worsened for 2 weeks, the patient underwent spinal MRI, which revealed extensive lesions that were concerning for metastases. A pathologic fracture at the eleventh thoracic vertebra (T11) was noted, with a pending pathologic fracture in the right femur. The patient was admitted to the hospital for workup and further imaging. Computed tomographic scan of her thorax showed mass-like consolidation in the left lower lobe with adjacent satellite nodularity and interlobular septal thickening, as well as multiple pulmonary nodules in the right lower lobe and enlarged hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated multifocal metastatic disease of the calvarium, infundibular masses, and a clival lesion. Computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy of the mass on the left lower lobe of the lung showed malignant cells in sheets with honeycomb pattern overlying a background of mucin. The cells possessed moderately vacuolated cytoplasm with round to oval pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei and prominent nucleoli, and tested positive for thyroid transcription factor–1 (TTF-1), cytokeratin 7 (CK7), caudal type homeobox 2 (CDX2), and cytokeratin 20 (CK20).
The patient was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma consistent with primary lung adenocarcinoma. Due to the pending pathologic fracture of the right hip, a decision to pursue right hip arthroplasty was made. However, the patient experienced gastric perforation 1 day after arthroplasty and developed rapid-onset oxygen desaturation associated with a drop in pulse and blood pressure that resulted in asystole and death. She had received no cancer treatment before her death. The findings at autopsy were consistent with metastatic adenocarcinoma, with the immediate cause of death being massive peritonitis from gastric perforation.
Formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE) specimens of primary lung tumor and metastatic tumor tissue from the brain of the patient, along with a fresh healthy cardiac muscle specimen, were obtained at the autopsy, which was performed 4 days after death. Genomic DNA and RNA were extracted and purified using AllPrep DNA/RNA Kits (QIAGEN). AmpliSeq for Illumina Focus Panel NGS assay was performed using the Illumina MiSeqDx instrument according to manufacturer instructions (Illumina). The AmpliSeq for Illumina Focus Panel is a targeted resequencing assay for biomarker analysis of 52 genes with known relevance to solid tumors including epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), KRAS, b-raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase (BRAF), erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 2 (ERBB2), ALK receptor tyrosine kinase (ALK), ROS proto-oncogene 1, receptor tyrosine kinase (ROS1), ret proto-oncogene (RET), mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK), neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase 1 (NTRK1), NTRK2, and NTRK3 routinely analyzed in the clinical management of NSCLC. A KRAS exon 2 p.G12D mutation was detected in the primary and metastatic tumor specimens but not in the benign tissue. Given the positive family history of lung cancer, the fresh normal cardiac muscle specimen was examined via whole-exome sequencing using SSELXT HS Human All Exon V8+NCV Kit (Agilent Technologies) on an Illumina NextSeq 550Dx instrument (Illumina). However, no variants of significance were identified.
CMA was performed using OncoScan microarray according to manufacturer instructions (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The OncoScan microarray consists of more than 220,000 probes that can detect DNA copy number alterations including gains, losses, and copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH). Results were investigated using the Chromosome Analysis Suite (ChAS; Thermo Fisher Scientific). The settings for the smallest copy number variation (CNV) regions in the ChAS were 50 Kb and 50 markers for gains, 25 Kb and 25 markers for losses, and 5 Mb for CN-LOH. CMA results for specimens from our patient revealed copy number gain at 1q21.1q44 and copy number losses of chromosomes 1p31.3p11.2, 6q, 9p, 19, and 22q in the primary and metastatic tumor specimens. These changes were not observed in the benign tissue from the patient, suggesting the somatic origin of the changes. Also, CNAs unique to the metastatic tumor specimen included copy number gains of chromosomes 8p12q24.3, 11q13.2q23.2, 12, and 15q22.2q26.3, as well as copy number losses of chromosomes 8p23.3p12, 9q22.32q34.11, and 11q23.2q25, suggesting their involvement in the metastatic process of tumor cells.
